title: Seizure and delirium secondary to carboplatin and pantoprazole therapy‐induced hypomagnesemia in a cancer patient
case_prompt:
A 62-year-old man with recently diagnosed squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue and hypopharynx presented after a 1-minute generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. He had a longstanding seizure disorder well controlled for 7 years on levetiracetam and had received his first cycle of carboplatin, abraxane, and pembrolizumab 18 days earlier. His medical history also included gastroesophageal reflux disease treated with oral pantoprazole.

On examination, he was drowsy but oriented, able to follow simple commands, with impaired attention and recall. He had generalized weakness (3/5 strength in all extremities) with preserved reflexes and no focal sensory or motor deficits. He was afebrile, and other vital signs were within normal limits. After an initial postictal confusion, his mental status deteriorated over the next 48 hours, with persistent agitation and confusion but no new focal findings.

Laboratory studies on presentation revealed: hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, WBC 3.4 K/μL, platelets 43 K/μL, lactate 5.9 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19 mmol/L, anion gap 19, calcium 6.1 mg/dL (corrected 6.8 mg/dL), potassium 3.5 mmol/L, and magnesium 0.7 mEq/L. Renal function and liver tests were unremarkable. Fractional excretion of magnesium was 24.9%. CT and MRI of the head were normal. A 24-hour video EEG showed mild-to-moderate diffuse cerebral dysfunction “nonspecific in etiology, but may be seen in the context of toxic-metabolic encephalopathies.”
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infectious causes were considered unlikely — “patient was afebrile, without elevated white blood cell count and his sepsis screen was unremarkable…”  
2. Structural or vascular lesions were excluded — “he did not have any sensory or motor neurodeficits with unremarkable imaging of the brain…”  
3. Nonconvulsive status epilepticus was ruled out — “Continuous vEEG was utilized to rule out non‐convulsive seizures.”  
4. Initial laboratory abnormalities raised concern for electrolyte-induced encephalopathy — “Initial common laboratory reports were significant for hypocalcemia and borderline hypokalemia.”  
5. Hypomagnesemia was identified as a unifying cause — “due to the patient’s recent exposure to platinum‐based chemotherapy agent, serum magnesium level was obtained which was low, at 0.7 mg/dl.”  
6. Renal magnesium wasting from carboplatin was confirmed — “fractional excretion of magnesium in urine was around 25% … confirmed … renal wasting of magnesium secondary to recent carboplatin exposure…”  
7. Proton pump inhibitor–induced hypomagnesemia was recognized as a contributor — “patient’s chronic use of oral pantoprazole was a likely contributor.”
